title: Triage workshop: console request logs & error analysis - Sunrise Education
summary: Redwood ran a hands-on triage workshop with Sunrise Education focused on using the Console to diagnose failing or slow requests. Demo covered request logs, trace view, error categorization, request playback, and linking traces to model variants and resource metrics. Primary customer concerns: reproducibility of failures, audit trails for SOC2, and whether playback reproduces KV-cache dependent issues. Agreed next steps: share security docs, run a 24-hour capture for production traffic, schedule a latency benchmarking PoC and follow up with cost/throughput options.
action_items: Ethan Park: Send security pack + SOC2 & network diagram; due 2025-11-03
Priya Desai: Provide a sample failing request ID and approximate time window; due 2025-10-30
Sara Li: Run a short playback in staging and capture logs, share steps; due 2025-11-05
next_steps: Redwood to email security package and whitepaper on playback guarantees
Customer to export example request IDs and grant a staging dataset window
Schedule 1-hour PoC benchmarking session (latency/cost) week of Nov 10
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-27
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Sara Li (Redwood SE), Jordan Alvarez (Redwood Product), Liam O'Connor (Sunrise Head of ML), Priya Desai (Platform Eng), Ava Martinez (SRE), Noah Chen (Security)

[00:00] Ethan Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and then we'll jump into a hands-on triage workflow in the Console. Sara, you want to kick us off?

[00:18] Sara Li: Yeah, thanks Ethan. Hi all — I'll share my screen. The goal is practical: show how you'd find a slow or errored request, understand why it happened, and then either replay it or gather the artifacts you need for a postmortem. We'll hit request logs, the trace waterfall, the error tags, and then playback.

[00:34] Priya Desai: Sounds good. We're seeing periodic failures in prod that sometimes don't reproduce in staging — so curious about the KV cache / prefix caching behavior you mentioned in docs.

[00:45] Sara Li: Perfect, that's actually a common gotcha. Quick note: transcription might mangle a few acronyms — K V cache might show up as K V cash — so apologies if the transcript looks funny.

[01:00] Jordan Alvarez: I'll jump in on why playback can differ: playback re-sends the request to a live model variant, but if state depends on in-memory KV cache or ephemeral context in the serving instance, it may behave differently unless we capture the cache snapshot. We'll show the console hints around that.

[01:20] Liam O'Connor: Great. Also our security team wants to know: will the playback store PII anywhere? We need assurance for SOC2.

[01:30] Noah Chen: Yeah, we need retention windows and whether playback creates artifacts in long-term logs or just ephemeral debug traces.

[01:40] Sara Li: Short answer: playback can be done in two modes — ephemeral replay (no long-term storage beyond a short debug window) or auditorily captured (for PoC if you want to reproduce over time). We'll show the flags. We'll also point you to the KMS integration and audit logs in the Console.

[02:05]
[02:10] --- Screen demo: Console home -> Requests -> Filter by status = error / latency > 2s ---

[02:22] Sara Li: Okay, here we filtered to show errors. You can see request IDs, model variant, region, and a high-level status. This table also surfaces a latency breakdown: queue time, model time, and network time. Notice that these two requests have large model time spikes.

[02:45] Ava Martinez: For those spikes, can we see GPU metrics on the same view? We had an incident where a particular node had throttling.

[02:55] Sara Li: You can. Click into a request -> hit the trace view -> on the right we pull host-level metrics (GPU utilization, memory pressure) as an attached timeline.

[03:10] [03:10] Sara Li: Opening trace: here's the waterfall. We have span rows for router, batcher, model-inference, and post-process. The model-inference span is tall. If you hover it, you get the kernel selection and quantization flags used — helpful for reproducing perf differences.

[03:36] Priya Desai: That hover text is very useful. It says quantization = int8 fastpath but we think in our cluster we were on int4; could that explain differences?

[03:46] Jordan Alvarez: Yes, different quantization or kernel paths can produce different latencies and slightly different outputs. Our smart routing may pick a compatible variant for latency fallback; the trace will show the actual deployed binary.

[04:02] [04:02] Sara Li: Also note the error tag: this request has a downstream 'timeout' flagged at the model-inference span. The Console annotates likely causes — in this case 'KV_CACHE_MISS + MODEL_TIMEOUT'.

[04:18] Liam O'Connor: If it's a KV cache miss, does playback re-warm the cache?

[04:24] Sara Li: Playback by default does not re-warm customer KV caches. We have an option to 'replay with cache snapshot' if you captured the prefix at time of failure. Otherwise you can do a controlled replay in a staging environment that shares cache or simulate the cache.

[04:38] Noah Chen: That needs to be explicit in our audit docs. We'll need the steps to capture a cache snapshot without exposing PII.

[04:47] Ethan Park: We'll include a doc on best practices — capture redacted context, or use hashed keys. We'll add that to the security pack.

[05:00] [05:00] --- Diving into a specific request ID: req_20251027_9876 ---

[05:12] Sara Li: Here's the request timeline. Timestamped events show request entering gateway, batch placement, model kernel start, model kernel end, response serialization. See the gap between model end and serialization — that's a post-processing Python hook that your team added (we can see 'post_hook: sentiment-normalize-v1').

[05:32] Priya Desai: That's our microservice doing additional NER. We saw intermittent spikes there. Are those hooks executed in the same host?

[05:39] Sara Li: They run in a sidecar process by default. You can configure whether to inline them or run async; Console's trace will show where the time is spent.

[05:50] Ava Martinez: Can we correlate that to CPU steal or container OOMs?

[05:56] Sara Li: Yes — the attached host timeline shows CPU steal and OOM events if they happened; we can overlay Kubernetes events.

[06:10] [06:10] --- Error classification & suggested next steps ---

[06:14] Sara Li: For an error, the Console will propose likely fixes based on heuristics: increase batch size tolerance, pin model to variant, enable auto-scale, or offload post-processing. It's advisory but it accelerates a first pass for the SE/Dev.

[06:30] Liam O'Connor: On the advisory text, does Redwood have confidence scores on the suggestions? We want to avoid blindly applying a change.

[06:38] Jordan Alvarez: Each suggestion has a confidence band — low/medium/high — based on past similar signals. We surface historical success rate when available.

[06:46] Priya Desai: Helpful. For change management we need to link any suggested config change to an audit trail entry.

[06:53] Sara Li: All Console changes generate an audit log entry tied to SSO identity; we'll demo that.

[07:00] [07:00] --- Playback demo ---

[07:04] Sara Li: I'm going to hit 'Replay' on this request. Options pop up: replay to live, replay to staging, replay with cache snapshot (if one exists). I'll choose replay to staging.

[07:20] [07:20] Sara Li: Replay launched. You can watch the live status; it maps the request through a new ephemeral router that mimics your route rules.

[07:30] Priya Desai: When you replay, are tokens re-counted for billing?

[07:35] Sara Li: Replays are accounted separately and appear in a debug usage bucket; they don't hit customer bill by default but can be optionally toggled to bill for end-to-end PoC.

[07:46] Ava Martinez: The replay completed with slightly different latency — 600ms vs 1.8s. Does the trace capture the model binary used?

[07:55] Sara Li: Yes, trace includes model binary hash and kernel metadata. Notice here that the original used variant v2-quant, while the replay hit v2-quant-fast. That explains the difference.

[08:10] Noah Chen: Can we lock the replay to a specific model binary?

[08:14] Sara Li: Yes, choose the 'pin model binary' checkbox. But again, if your production instance had an in-memory cache we didn't snapshot, results may still differ.

[08:26] [08:26] --- Deep-dive: debugging a non-deterministic failure ---

[08:30] Sara Li: Non-determinism often comes from three places: ephemeral KV state, race in hook code, or cross-request contamination from shared hosts. We'll search the request window for other concurrent requests that shared the same host.

[08:45] [08:45] Sara Li: See this heatmap — multiple high-latency requests overlap on host i-09-xyz around 14:03 UTC. That suggests noisy neighbor.

[08:55] Priya Desai: We do run batch-heavy jobs at midnight — could be a scheduling collision.

[09:00] Ethan Park: If you'd like, Redwood can run a capture for a 24-hour window and send anonymized traces to analyze peak contention patterns.

[09:10] Liam O'Connor: That would be useful. We also want a short writeup that links these host-level spikes to remediation steps.

[09:18] Jordan Alvarez: We'll include recommended fixes — adjust autoscaler thresholds, isolate critical routes to Dedicated capacity, or use a node-affinity rule.

[09:28] [09:28] --- Security & compliance notes ---

[09:30] Noah Chen: Quick security question — is replay data encrypted at rest and who has access?

[09:36] Sara Li: Replays and debug traces are encrypted with your integrated KMS if you opt in; access is RBAC-protected and all accesses are audited. We'll provide the full matrix in the security pack.

[09:46] Noah Chen: And retention? Default retention is 30 days?

[09:50] Sara Li: Defaults can be configured per workspace. For enterprises we often set 90-day or shorter, and we support redact-on-ingest for sensitive fields.

[10:00] [10:00] --- Live troubleshooting scenario (customer-supplied example) ---

[10:04] Priya Desai: We provided an example request id earlier via email; can we try to locate it? It's around 2025-10-20 02:12 UTC.

[10:12] Ethan Park: Let's use the filter. (typing) Found it: req_20251020_4412. It's marked as 'partial render' and has a large post-process time.

[10:26] Sara Li: Opening trace for that req_4412 — I see the model took 400ms, but the post-process hook took 1600ms and threw a JSON parse warning at the tail. That matches your logs snippet that had a 'json decode error'.

[10:44] Priya Desai: That hook code expects a list of tokens and trips on certain edge cases. So this is likely our bug. But sometimes we don't have enough context to reproduce.

[10:54] Sara Li: You can download the full debug bundle (redacted) from the Console and share with your dev team. It includes the input, trace, host metrics, and model binary hash.

[11:08] Ava Martinez: We'll take that and test.

[11:12] [11:12] --- Notes on integration: request sampling and cost controls ---

[11:16] Jordan Alvarez: For heavy production, enable targeted sampling for error classes and high-latency traces to limit storage and cost. Optimize will recommend sampling rates depending on the error rate.

[11:28] Liam O'Connor: Does Optimize recommend batching adjustments? Our cost per token spiked last month.

[11:34] Jordan Alvarez: Yes — Optimize will analyze sequence length distribution and recommend batching windows and quantization profiles. We'll show a sample Optimize report in follow-up.

[11:44] Priya Desai: Could Optimize also recommend when to move a route to Dedicated?

[11:48] Jordan Alvarez: It can. If you have consistent peak throughput above a threshold, Optimize will flag potential cost savings and suggest dedicated sizing.

[12:00] [12:00] --- Wrap-up and recap ---

[12:03] Ethan Park: Quick recap: we showed request inspector, trace waterfall, error classification, playback options, and host metric overlays. Action items we captured: security pack, sample request capture, and a staging playback trial. Anything else?

[12:18] Liam O'Connor: Please include the exact steps for capturing a KV cache snapshot or the recommended workaround (hash keys).

[12:25] Ethan Park: We'll include that. Also we'll include the Optimize preview for batching and dedicated sizing.

[12:34] Priya Desai: And can we get the replay logs in a format we can feed into our incident platform? We want a JSON export that maps to our schema.

[12:42] Sara Li: Yes — Console export includes JSON and CSV. We'll send a sample mapping.

[12:50] Ava Martinez: Thanks — this was really practical.

[12:53] Ethan Park: Great. We'll follow up with the security pack and schedule the PoC benchmarking. Thanks everyone.

[12:58] --- End meeting ---

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-attributed speaker labels and small ASR errors (e.g., K V cache -> "K V cash"), some punctuation oddities.
